title: Photo-enhanced CO2 hydrogenation by plasmonic Cu/ZnO at atmospheric pressure
abstract: The photo-assisted carbon dioxide (CO2) hydrogenation provides an efficient and straightforward method for producing solar fuels with high efficiency. However, the development of highly efficient catalysts with controllable selectivity and long-term stability still faces major challenges. This study proves that solar energy can promote the CO2 hydrogenation over Cu/ZnO catalysts efficiently at atmospheric pressure and the selectivity of the reduction products can be controlled by varying the Cu/Zn molar ratio. Meanwhile, the hot electrons generated from Cu nanoparticles due to the surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and the photogenerated electrons from ZnO with light excitation can promote the H2 cleavage and the activation of CO2.
paragraphs: The development of chemical industry is inseparable from the burning of fossil fuels. However, this dependence on fossil fuels releases a large amount of CO2, triggering the greenhouse effect. Therefore, it is of great significance to convert CO2 into high-calorie fuels, which can both reduce global warming and alleviate the energy crisis. Generally speaking, there are many ways to convert CO2 into fuel. An attractive way is to reduce CO2 into C1 products through hydrogenation, making use of H2 from renewable resources. Among the C1 products, carbon monoxide (CO), methanol (CH3OH) and methane (CH4) are widely used as fuels or chemical raw materials, occupying a prominent position in the industry. Thus, there has been increasing interest in the design of highly active and selective catalysts that convert CO2 into C1 products.

Among the catalysts for CO2 hydrogenation, Cu/ZnO prepared by co-precipitation method has been regarded as one of the most efficient catalysts in terms of both turn-over frequency (TOF, based on Cu active sites) and product yield. However, the catalytic reactions are normally carried out at a high temperature of 200–300 ​°C and a high pressure of 5.0–10.0 ​MPa. Besides, the stability of the catalysts under harsh conditions also needs to be improved. Recently, researches demonstrate that the introduction of light energy can improve the performance of conventional thermal catalysis significantly. In these cases, the light was utilized as an additional stimulus to reduce the barrier of CO2 hydrogenation through the mechanism of electron-driven catalytic reactions. Nevertheless, there are still several issues need to be improved, including limited performance enhancement with light, low selectivity of reduction products and unclear catalytic mechanism.

In this work, a Cu/ZnO catalyst was synthesized for the CO2 hydrogenation at atmospheric pressure, which exhibit highly-enhanced CO2 hydrogenation performance with light energy. Notably, the catalytic activity was 10.4 times higher than that of thermal catalysis without light irradiation and the production rate was 300 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1. Moreover, the catalytic products can be selectively controlled by varying the molar ratio of Cu/Zn. The performance enhancement was attributed to the synergistic effect of Cu and ZnO, which was verified by the wavelength and component-dependent measurements. The findings obtained here provide a promising strategy for improving the conventional thermal catalytic reactions with light energy.

Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (99.9%), Cu(NO3)2·3H2O (99.9%)and Na2CO3 (99.9%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Ethanol was purchased from FuYu Chemical. All Chemicals were used without any purification.

The Cu/ZnO catalysts was mainly prepared through the following three steps: the precursor was prepared by a simple precipitation method, then the metal oxide was obtained after calcination by air, and the final target catalysts were obtained by reduction via argon (Ar) containing 5% H2 by volume. Firstly, a certain amount of Cu(NO3)2·3H2O and Zn(NO3)2·6H2O, with a fixed molar ratio, as listed in Table S1, were dissolved into 10 ​mL of deionized water, named solution A. Secondly, the corresponding molar amount of Na2CO3 was dissolved into 20 ​mL of deionized water and stirred to form a clear and transparent Na2CO3 solution, named solution B. Then the solution B was added into the solution A as a precipitator under vigorous stirring at 60 ​°C. The obtained suspension was heated and stirred at 60 ​°C for 2 ​h and then aged at room temperature overnight. Then it was filtered and washed thoroughly with deionized water and dried at 110 ​°C for 6 ​h. The dried samples were ground and then calcined at 350 ​°C for 4 ​h with a heating rate of 10 ​°C min−1. Finally, the obtained metal oxides were calcined at 300 ​°C for 3 ​h in a tube furnace containing 5% H2 in an Ar atmosphere with a heating rate of 5 ​°C min−1. In addition, two comparative catalysts were prepared in a similar way, namely Cu and ZnO.

The crystal structure of the Cu/ZnO catalysts were obtained via X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) by a Bruker AXS D8 with Cu Kα radiation (λ ​= ​1.5406 ​Å). A scanning electron microscope (SEM, Hitachi S-4800) was used to analyze the element map of the sample. The morphology and lattice distance of the samples were observed using a transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEOL-2100). Chemical valence analysis was obtained via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) by a Thermo Fisher Scientific (Esclab 250) spectrometer and all binding energies were corrected by the C 1s peaks (284.8 ​eV) of the surface of adventitious carbon. UV–vis absorption spectra were carried out on a UV–vis spectrophotometer (UV-2600, Shimadzu, Japan) possessing integrating sphere using Barium sulfate as a reference sample. The Brunauer-Emmet-Teller (BET) surface areas of the sample was measured by A Micromeritics ASAP 2020 analyzer, and the pretreatment was carried out at 150 ​°C under vacuum for 4 ​h.

The CO2 hydrogenation performance test was carried out in a fixed-bed reactor (Fig. S1) with a volume of about 160 ​mL ​at normal pressure, and each experiment used 50 ​mg of catalyst. The hydrogenation of CO2 reaction was carried out at atmospheric pressure in the temperature of 300 ​°C, which was precisely controlled by a JF-956 ​S controller (JFT001S) with a thermocouple in the fixed bed reactor. The light source used in the photo-assisted reaction was a 300 ​W xenon arc lamp (AULTT CEL-HXF300, Beijing China Education Au-light Co., Ltd) equipped with 420 ​nm cutoff filter was used as the light source (λ ​> ​420 ​nm) in subsequent experiments. Before the reaction, high-purity Ar with a flow rate of 10 ​mL min-1 was used to exhaust the air inside the reactor for 30 ​min. Then 5 ​mL of CO2 and 20 ​mL of H2 were injected into the reactor as reactants. 0.2 ​mL gas was extracted per hour by an injector and analyzed with an online gas chromatograph (GC-7920 and GC-2030, Shimadzu, Japan). In this experiment, the reduction products mainly included CO and CH4. In order to exclude the possibility that the carbon products were from CO2 reduction and not from the catalyst itself or external pollution, we used an atmosphere filled with argon as the reactant instead of CO2 and H2 in a controlled experiment. The results showed that no products were detected in the controlled experiment for Cu/ZnO catalysts, as shown in Fig. S2.

A series of physical and chemical properties were characterized for the catalyst with Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/1. The XRD pattern of the Cu/ZnO catalyst before reaction was shown in Fig. 1 a. All the diffraction peaks are in good agreement with ZnO (JCPDS. NO. 89–511) and Cu (JCPDS. NO. 85–1326) profile, indicating Cu/ZnO catalyst was successfully synthesized and had good crystallinity. The diffraction peaks at 43.38°, 50.56° and 74.26° correspond to (111), (100) and (110) crystallography planes of the metallic Cu, respectively. While the diffraction peaks at 31.77°, 34.44°, 36.30°, 47.56°, 56.64°, 62.94°, 68.06°, 72.72°, 77.06° and 81.57° correspond to (100), (002), (101), (102), (110), (103), (112), (004), (202) and (104) crystallography planes of ZnO, respectively. The optical properties of the samples were measured before studying the photothermal catalytic reaction. Fig. 1b shows the UV–vis absorption spectra of the Cu/ZnO catalyst, metallic Cu and ZnO support. Bare ZnO nanoparticles only show an intense and broad absorption from 200 to 450 ​nm with the maximum absorption peak at 372 ​nm, indicating ZnO only absorbs UV light effectively. There are two strong absorption peaks at 387.5 ​nm and 578.6 ​nm on the Cu/ZnO catalyst, which correspond to the absorption of the ZnO and the LSPR absorption of Cu nanoparticles, respectively. The strong light absorption demonstrates that efficient use of the solar energy would be feasible. It is noteworthy to mention that the absorption peak of Cu nanoparticles in the visible light range was relatively broad, which might be due to light surface oxidation and the agglomeration of Cu nanoparticles.

As shown in Fig. 1c, the N2 adsorption and desorption isotherms were part of type VI, demonstrating mesoporous characteristics of the Cu/ZnO catalysts. The specific surface area of 43.05 ​m2 ​g−1 is basically the same as reported in the literature. The surface composition and the chemical environment of all elements on the surface of the catalysts were characterized by means of XPS measurements. Fig. 1d depicts the total XPS survey spectrum of the Cu/ZnO catalyst, indicating the presence of Cu, Zn and O elements. The Cu 2p (Fig. 1e) spectrum exhibits two main peaks at 933.4 ​eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 953.2 ​eV (Cu 2p1/2) with two corresponding satellite peaks respectively. Specifically, the peaks at 933.4 ​eV and 953.2 ​eV with a spin-orbital doublet splitting (Δ) of 19.8 ​eV can be indexed to the Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 in its zero-valence state. Fig. 1f shows the high-resolution XPS spectra of the Zn 2p region. Due to spin-orbit coupling, each spectrum consists of two main Zn 2p components at the position of 1020.28 ​eV (Zn 2p3/2) and 1043.29 ​eV (Zn 2p1/2). These binding energies are representative of the Zn2+ ions in the oxygen environment, which is very similar to previous studies. All these results indicate that the presence of Zn2+ oxidation and metallic Cu states on the surface of the sample.

Scanning electron micrograph (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of the Cu/ZnO catalyst before reaction were shown in Fig. 2 . The SEM image (Fig. 2a) shows that the catalyst exhibits as relatively uniform solid small particles. SEM images of catalysts with different Cu/Zn molar ratios (Fig. S3) show that these catalysts have little difference with each other in terms of morphology, except that the particle size is slightly larger when the ratio is 1/2. TEM image of the catalyst was shown in Fig. 2b. It shows that the darker areas are Cu and the lighter areas are ZnO. It can be seen that the size of Cu nanoparticles is about 5 ​nm and the size of ZnO is between 25 and 40 ​nm, showing that as-prepared catalysts are of small particle size and low dispersion nature. The TEM contrast images of Cu/Zn 1/1 and 1/2 were shown in Fig. S4. It can be seen that the black areas of Cu/Zn 1/1 were larger than that of 1/2, which indicates that the Cu content is more at this ratio. The HRTEM image reveals that the lattice spacing was 0.260 ​nm and 0.208 ​nm for Cu/ZnO, which correspond to (002) crystal plane of ZnO and (111) crystal plane of Cu, respectively (Fig. 2c). These results are consistent with the XRD patterns. More importantly, it is worth noting that there was a close contact between Cu and ZnO nanoparticles, this is conducive to the progress of catalytic reaction. Energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) elemental mapping images (Fig. 2d) confirm the uniform distribution of Cu, Zn and O elements in the Cu/ZnO catalyst.

Firstly, the Cu/ZnO catalyst with Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/1 was employed study the effect of photo energy on thermal catalytic CO2 hydrogenation performance at atmospheric pressure. The CO2 reduction performance of the catalyst under pure photo, pure thermal and photothermal conditions was shown in Fig. 3 a (A 300 ​W xenon arc lamp without filters was used as the light source). It was shown that there was no activity under pure photo conditions for CO2 hydrogenation reduction, whereas for samples under pure thermal and photothermal conditions, main product was CO and the production rates were 28.8 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and 300 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1, respectively. The photothermal catalytic system exhibits more efficient reduction of CO2 than the thermal catalytic system for Cu/ZnO catalysts. Surprisingly, it can be seen that the yield of CO under photothermal conditions was 10.4 times higher than the rate under pure thermal conditions, indicating that there was a significant enhancement on the catalytic reaction due to the introduction of light. Such an enhancement was not just a simple heating effect of light irradiation. This might be the fact that the electrons generated from Cu nanoparticles due to the surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and the photogenerated electrons from ZnO with light excitation can promote the activation of CO2. Meanwhile, the self-reduction of the oxidation state of the surface layer of copper after light excitation keeps the surface in a metallic state, which is also conducive to catalytic reaction. The results of three cycles of stability experiments were shown in Fig. 3b. It can be seen that the reduction products obtained from these three repeated experiments were all CO and the yields remained stable. Fig. 3c shows the increase of CO with time in three repeated experiments, indicating that the increase of CO is linear and the catalysts possess excellent stability. Fig. 3d shows a comparison experiment between Cu/ZnO catalyst, metallic Cu and ZnO under photothermal conditions for CO2 hydrogenation reduction. The results show that the photothermal CO2 reduction product of ZnO was mainly CO with the production rate of 4.66 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and the product of metallic Cu was mainly CH4 with the production rate of 4.6 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1. This shows that it didn’t show excellent photothermal CO2 hydrogenation performance when Cu or ZnO was individually used as catalyst. It can be inferred that the performance enhancement after light introduction was due to the synergistic effect of Cu and ZnO. Fig. 3e shows the photothermal CO2 hydrogenation reduction performance of the catalyst under different wavelengths of light, including UV light (λ ​< ​420 ​nm), Vis-IR light (λ ​> ​420 ​nm) and UV–Vis-IR light. It was worth noting that the reduction products include both CO and CH4 under UV light, the rates were 28.25 ​μmol ​g−1 h−1and 25.49 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1, respectively. For Vis-IR light conditions, the products were mainly CO with the rate of 27.55 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and CH4 with the rate of 2.99 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1. Most importantly, the product was only CO under UV–Vis-IR light with the rate of 246.54 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1, far exceeding the rates under the first two conditions. In other words, only under UV–Vis-IR light irradiation can the CO2 reduction performance be greatly improved. In general, the results from Fig. 3d and e shows that this enhancement is based on the synergistic photoactivation of Cu and ZnO under UV–Vis-IR light. Excitation of Cu and ZnO simultaneously is essential to promote the process of synergistic CO2 hydrogenation, since the significant enhancement occurs only with the light containing both bands. Under the dual excitation of Cu and ZnO, electrons from both plasmon excitation of Cu and band gap excitation of ZnO can accelerate H2 cleavage and CO2 adsorption and promote the catalytic reaction. Meanwhile, ZnO promotes the stabilization of CO2 hydrogenation intermediates, while Cu facilitates the adsorption and cracking of H2 on the surface during catalysis. In order to prove that single Cu or ZnO does not have the above-mentioned high-efficiency photothermal CO2 reduction ability, supplementary comparison experiments were carried out on Cu or ZnO separately under photo, thermal and photothermal conditions. The results were shown in Fig. S5, indicating that the photothermal catalytic system does not improve the CO2 reduction performance significantly with Cu or ZnO compared with the thermal catalytic system. The strengthened part may only be due to the local temperature increase caused by light irradiation. Then the effect of light intensity on the performance were studied. As shown in Fig. 3f, the rate of CO evolution increases as increasing the light intensity and the contribution of light energy to the reaction also increases. Thus, the enhanced catalytic activity positively related to the optical density indicates the reaction promoted by the light energy. Fig. S6 shows the XRD patterns before and after the reaction, indicating unchanged structure and stable phase composition, proving that the catalysts have excellent chemical stability.

To explore the influence of the Cu/Zn molar ratio on the product selectivity of the photothermal CO2 reduction reaction, a series of control experiments with different Cu/Zn molar ratio were conducted. The XRD patterns of the samples were shown in Fig. 4 a and Fig. 4b. The results show that the corresponding peak height of Cu decreases successively from bottom to top, which means the crystallinity of copper decreases with the decrease of copper proportion. The catalytic performance test results were shown in Fig. 4c. It displays that the photothermal CO2 reduction products were only CO for samples with Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/1 and 1/4, and the rates were 300 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and 223.6 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1. Whereas the product was only CH4 over sample with Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/2, and the rate was 51.93 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1. In addition, the products were both CO and CH4 over sample with the Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/3, and the rates were 66 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and 13 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1, respectively. The above dates indicate the Cu/Zn molar ratio can influence the selectivity of photothermal CO2 reduction, which may be related to the relative content of copper and the binding mode between Cu and ZnO. The Cu 2p and Zn 2p XPS spectra of catalysts with different Cu/Zn molar ratios were shown in Fig. S7. It shows that there is no significant difference in the binding energy of samples with different proportions. In order to explore the effect of the Cu/Zn molar ratio on its performance, the performance of other four ratios between 1/1 and 1/2 were further studied, as shown in Fig. 4d. The results show that as the proportion of Cu decreases, the total amount of products gradually decreases but the proportion of CH4 gradually increases. Therefore, it can be inferred that the CO2 selectivity between 1/1 and 1/2 was a gradual process rather than a sudden change. According to our experimental results and analysis, we conclude that the content of Cu and particle size as well as the binding state of Cu/ZnO might play an important role in CO2 reduction yield and selectivity.

Secondly, in order to further investigate the superior photothermal synergistic effects of the Cu/ZnO catalyst, a series of tests were also carried out on sample with Cu/Zn molar ratio of 1/2. No product was detected under pure light conditions, which was shown in Fig. 5 a. Interestingly, the product at this ratio was 100% CH4 under pure thermal and photothermal conditions with the production rates of 6.876 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1 and 51.9 ​μmol ​g−1 ​h−1, respectively. The performance was improved by 7.5 times. Fig. 5b shows stability test for Cu/Zn 1/2 and Fig. 5c displays the increase of CH4 with time in three repeated experiments. These results all suggest that the reduction products were only CH4 and the yields remained stable, which increased almost linearly with time. The XRD patterns before and after reaction shows the stable structure and phase composition of the catalyst (Fig. S8). Furthermore, Fig. 5d shows the change of the product with time under certain conditions (3 ​h in dark and followed by 3 ​h in light at 300 ​°C). At first, it shows that the CH4 increased at a very slow rate under dark conditions and there was a small amout of CO produced. Then CO gradually disappeared after adding light and the CH4 increased significantly. These findings all indicate that light can greatly improve the performance of CO2 hydrogenation in thermal catalysis, which is in accordance with the results when the Cu/Zn molar ratio is 1/1.

In summary, the results show that the light can significantly promote the thermal catalytic CO2 hydrogenation over Cu/ZnO catalyst at atmospheric pressure. Under UV–Vis-IR irradiation, electrons from both plasmon excitation of Cu and band gap excitation of ZnO can accelerate H2 cleavage and CO2 adsorption and promote the catalytic reaction. Meanwhile, the self-reduction of the oxidation state of the surface layer of copper after light excitation keeps the surface in a metallic state, which is also conducive to catalytic reaction. Moreover, the selectivity of the reaction product can be adjusted by varying the Cu/Zn molar ratio of the catalysts. This might change the number as well as the state of active sites, moreover, the binding state of Cu and ZnO can be changed by changing the content of Cu, which results in altered products selectivity. This research is of crucial significance for plasma-enhanced photothermal catalysis, which holds promise in enhancing traditional catalysis which uses heating as main energy source.
